What was meant to be the ultimate demonstration of the military superiority of the United States and Israel has turned into a major political and strategic defeat for Donald Trump.At the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, the American president attempted to present the 14-point draft agreement as a diplomatic success. Yet the very content of the agreement tells a different story: Washington failed to achieve regime change, failed to destroy Iran’s offensive capabilities, and ultimately found itself compelled to negotiate with the very power it had sought to overthrow.The implicit objective of the United States and Israel was regime change. That objective failed.Even after the elimination of key figures within the Iranian system, the Islamic Republic did not collapse. On the contrary, like a hydra, it repeatedly regenerated itself: less centralized command, more power distributed among the Revolutionary Guards, the security apparatus, and the new religious leadership.The succession of Mojtaba Khamenei, son of the previous Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, marked not a normalization but rather a further transformation of the regime in a more security-oriented and militarized direction.Nor did the promised military victory materialize. Joint American and Israeli strikes were supposed to eliminate Iran’s offensive capabilities. They did not. Iran emerged weakened but not neutralized: it continued producing and launching low-cost missiles and drones, struck or threatened American bases and infrastructure in the Gulf, and above all used the Strait of Hormuz as a strategic weapon to demonstrate that it could still shake the global economy.The 14 Points of the AgreementAccording to reports leaked to the international press, the draft agreement includes:1. An immediate and permanent ceasefire.

2. A U.S. commitment to respect Iranian

sovereignty.

3. Full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping.

4. An end to naval restrictions imposed by the United States during the conflict.

5. The resumption of Iranian oil exports.

6. Partial suspension of U.S. sanctions on Iranian oil during a 60-day negotiation period.

7. The gradual unfreezing of Iranian assets held abroad.

8. An initial transfer of a significant portion of those funds.

9. The opening of final negotiations lasting 60 days.

10. An Iranian commitment not to develop nuclear weapons.

11. Subsequent discussions regarding enriched uranium and enrichment activities.

12. An investment and economic reconstruction plan for Iran.

13. Gradual normalization of economic relations between Iran and the international community.

14. A final agreement addressing, in a comprehensive manner, nuclear issues, sanctions, and economic reconstruction.If the true objectives of the war were regime change, the destruction of Iran’s military capabilities, and Tehran’s unconditional submission, then it is difficult to interpret this draft as an American victory.

On the contrary, the document appears to represent an implicit recognition of the necessity of negotiating with the Islamic Republic and its leadership, which survived the conflict.What Are the Consequences of the Peace Agreement and the End of the Conflict? Let’s see them together:1. American Defeat and Growing IsolationThis represents one of the most serious strategic setbacks suffered by the United States in recent decades. Not because Iran “won” militarily in the conventional sense, but because Washington failed to achieve its political objectives. The Iranian regime remains in power, and its missile capabilities have not been destroyed.The Strait of Hormuz has become a bargaining tool in Tehran’s hands. Washington proved unable to impose surrender and was forced to accept a draft agreement involving not only the reopening of the strait but also the easing of oil sanctions and the possible release of frozen Iranian funds.Even more significant is the international context. Apart from Israel, no country truly wished to be dragged into a war against Iran.Europe maintained a cautious position and preferred de-escalation over direct intervention, partly because participating in a conflict lacking a convincing casus belli would have undermined the soft power that the European Union has sought to build in recent years.As a result, the United States found itself far more isolated than it had been accustomed to during major international crises of the past.2. The Crisis of American Soft Power and Hard PowerThe decline of American soft power had begun long ago. China has steadily expanded its economic, technological, and diplomatic influence across vast regions of the globe. Meanwhile, political polarization within the United States and the increasing unpredictability of Washington’s foreign policy have weakened the confidence of many allies.But this war revealed something deeper. It is not only soft power that has entered into crisis. For the first time in many years, American coercive power has also shown clear limitations.The supremacy of the so-called “American Century” rested on two pillars: military and technological superiority on one side, and cultural, economic, and symbolic attraction on the other. Hollywood, Silicon Valley, the dollar, American universities, and the worldwide network of military bases formed the core of this hegemony for decades.However, if this structure proves unable to impose its will on a country subjected for years to economic sanctions, international isolation, and military pressure, then the message sent to the rest of the world becomes unavoidable: the United States remains the greatest power on Earth, but it is no longer an irresistible power.3. The Strengthening of the Iranian RegimeParadoxically, the conflict risks strengthening the Iranian regime.Not economically, where the country remains weakened and scarred by war, but politically and symbolically. External attempts to overthrow governments that end in failure often reinforce narratives of national resistance.The Islamic Republic will be able to present itself as the country that withstood the attacks of the world’s leading superpower and compelled it to sit down at the negotiating table.Furthermore, the war has likely accelerated Iran’s transformation into an even more security-oriented state. The Revolutionary Guards emerge from the conflict with greater political influence, while the new leadership inherits a country that perceives itself as under siege and therefore more willing to accept a greater concentration of power.4. Israel’s Growing IsolationIsrael emerges from this war in a position of profound weakness, aggravated by its attempts to undermine negotiations through continued and intense bombings in Lebanon.While it still enjoys overwhelming military superiority over its neighbors, it continues to experience an increasingly severe deterioration of its international image, one that may prove almost irreversible.The devastation in Gaza, the increasingly vocal accusations coming from numerous international organizations, and the growing hostility of global public opinion have eroded a significant portion of the moral legitimacy Israel had enjoyed in the West for decades.The challenge for Tel Aviv is that even its principal ally, the United States, has demonstrated limitations that would have seemed unimaginable only a few years ago. If Washington is compelled to negotiate with Tehran, if Europe refuses to enter the war, and if much of the world increasingly turns toward emerging powers, then Israel too must contend with an international environment far less favorable than in the past.Although this does not necessarily signify the definitive end of American supremacy, it nevertheless confronts us with what historians may one day regard as one of the clearest signs of the gradual decline of the American Century.
